submitter: bugs_open/275 — bugfix_275_silent_row_caps lane. Filed 2026-08-14 by webdesign_uk_build_service; unowned until today (who-owns.py names the FILING lane only; no live session transcript mentions 275).
rationale:
bugs_open/275: tool-suggester's load_library_tools ends `ORDER BY display_name LIMIT 30` against a library of 74 masters, so the model deciding which tools a site should have is shown 30 of 74 — and which 44 are hidden is an accident of the alphabet, not a judgement of relevance.

IT IS A SILENT CAP, which is the whole reason it survived. An LLM returns plausible suggestions whether it saw 30 rows or 74. There is no wrong output to notice, no error, no truncation marker. The only way to find it is to read the SQL.

MEASURED 2026-08-16, and WORSE THAN FILED. At filing: 68 masters, 38 hidden. Today: 74 masters, 44 hidden — the library grows, so the damage grows with it. A refinement the bug did not make: migration 406's requires-backend gate is NOT the cause and barely narrows anything — exactly 1 of 74 masters carries the tag and 3 of 40 sites have the capability. The cap is doing all of the hiding.

WHY THE FIX IS NOT SIMPLY 'REMOVE THE LIMIT'. The cap was not purely arbitrary: 74 rows is 37,209 chars of prompt (~9-10k tokens). The bug's own candidate 1 says 'if the real constraint is prompt size, cap by TOKENS at the prompt assembly, not by row count in the dark' — and the data says exactly which knob to turn:
  description   29,832 chars across 74 rows  <-- 80% of the payload
  id             2,664 | display_name 2,100 | function 1,828 | category 785
description: median 374, mean 403, max 2,526; 50 of 74 exceed 200 chars.
  TODAY  30 rows (41% of library), description uncapped -> 16,421 chars
  THIS   74 rows (100%),           description <= 200   -> 20,376 chars
So: THE WHOLE LIBRARY FOR +24% PAYLOAD (~4,000 chars, ~1k tokens). That is arithmetic on live data, not a preference. 200 was checked for MEANING as well as size — the first 200 chars of the longest descriptions still say what the tool IS ('The Arena is Spark's competitive mode, v1 as a fully self-contained client-side experience...'), which is what a relevance judgement needs. I read the prompt template rather than assuming: it renders `- {{.display_name}} ({{.function}}, id: {{.id}}): {{.description}}`.

THE FRAMEWORK HALF, AND WHY IT IS THE LARGER PART OF THIS SUBMISSION. The standing instruction on this tree is to prefer a fix applicable to the framework over the individual case. 275 is one instance of a class: a row-count LIMIT feeding an LLM prompt is silent by construction. Census over live agent_definitions: 26 literal LIMITs in query-shaped step configs, of which SEVEN are multi-row caps that can bite this way — tool-suggester.load_library_tools 30, internal-linker.load_candidate_pages 15, model-directory-trigger.find_directory_sites 12, tool-recreation-handler.load_related_context 10, content-feed-trigger.find_news_sites 5, visual-design-auditor.load_design_context 5, fix-proposer.load_last_bundle 2. EVERY ONE runs through QueryDatabaseAction. So the detection goes there, once, and the whole class becomes visible — including caps nobody has written yet.

ANSWERING THE ARCHITECTURE SIGNAL THE PRE-COMMIT HOOK RAISED ('migration + platform code in one commit — needs a staged rollout order'). THERE IS NO ORDERING CONSTRAINT AND I AM NOT CLAIMING ONE (owner ruling 2026-07-29 §2 retired condition (1) precisely because threads were inventing these). The two halves are INDEPENDENT: the Go change is observational and works against any query, capped or not; the migration is config-only and works against any binary, warning or not. Neither reads the other. Applying either alone leaves a coherent system — the migration alone fixes 275, the Go change alone makes the other six caps visible.

AND WHY PART A IS NOT ARCHITECTURE-SCOPE. It adds no field, no key, no contract, no capability. It cannot change a query, a result, or a row — it emits a log line. Under the 2026-07-29 §1 ruling the RFC trigger is 'does it change what the shared mechanism GUARANTEES', and QueryDatabaseAction's guarantee (run this query, return these rows) is byte-identical afterwards. Under the 2026-08-02 §2 / RFC_010 rule that new authority on a shared seam must ship opt-in with the unsafe default OFF: a warning takes no authority, so there is nothing to gate. This is deliberately the weakest intervention that makes the class visible; the stronger one (a LIMIT n+1 probe that would report '30 of 74' definitively) DOES change what a shared action returns, and is recorded as the follow-up rather than smuggled in here.

THE SIGNAL-TO-NOISE DECISION, stated because it is the arm most likely to be 'simplified' later: LIMIT 1 is excluded. 19 of the 26 live hits are the fetch-one/claim-one idiom (load_brief, claim_item, load_tool, load_diagnosis...), which return exactly one row BY DESIGN on every execution. Including them would emit a warning per run for ever and train every reader to ignore the channel. The cost is stated rather than hidden: a genuine one-row truncation is invisible to this check.

REUSE CHECKED BEFORE WRITING — this is the objection the reuse_agent seat gated bugs_open/257 on, and I am not repeating it. grep over platform/ finds no existing LIMIT parsing or result-cap detection: the Truncate* family is string truncation, markTruncated is LLM stop_reason handling, LimitedRead is HTTP body bounding, isTruncatedJSON is JSON well-formedness. Nothing to reuse — checked, not assumed.

MUTATION TESTING — nine mutations, all killed, and TWO of them changed the code. M3 (`==` -> `>=`) SURVIVED: a driver cannot return more rows than its own LIMIT, so the two are equivalent for every reachable input. Rather than record an equivalent mutant and move on, I switched to the defensive `>=` WITH the reasoning in the source and a test pinning the arm, because the second caller this helper does not have yet (a merged set, a retried page) would silently lose the signal under `==`. M7 (unwire the warning from the action) SURVIVED until a CALL-SITE test existed — every other test passed while the action never called the helper, which is this estate's own 'the helper being correct and the helper being USED are independent facts'. That test is behavioural (sqlmock + zap observer), not a source scan, because register OPP-003 records a source-scanning detector that examined zero files and printed a clean result.

plan.summary: Two independent halves. (A) FRAMEWORK: QueryDatabaseAction warns when a result set is exactly as large as its query's own literal LIMIT (n>=2), naming the step — observational only, no behaviour change, making all seven live multi-row caps and every future one visible at the single point they share. (B) THIS BUG: migration 445 gives tool-suggester the whole 74-tool library by bounding `description` at 200 chars instead of bounding coverage at 30 rows — measured as +24% payload for +147% coverage — preserving migration 406's requires-backend gate byte-for-byte, scoped by id with a pre-state gate.

edits.rationale: The detector, in its own file so the reasoning travels with it. The regex is ANCHORED TO THE END of the statement: only a trailing LIMIT bounds the whole result set, and a LIMIT inside a subquery or CTE bounds something else entirely — warning on that would be false. A parameterised `LIMIT $2` deliberately does not match, because there is no literal to compare and a guess produces a warning nobody can act on. n<2 is excluded (the fetch-one idiom, 19 of 26 live hits). resultHitItsRowCap uses `>=` not `==`: equivalent for every input reachable today, chosen so a future caller whose row count did not come straight from the driver cannot silently lose the signal — with that reasoning in the source, because mutation M3 proved the choice is otherwise untestable and reads as arbitrary.

The one point all 26 query-shaped steps pass through. It already logs the row count and says nothing about whether that count hit a ceiling — so a truncated view and a complete one produce identical output, which is the defect. Added immediately after the existing Complete log, as a WARN carrying step, agent_type, limit and rows_returned: an unattributed cap warning tells nobody which query to go and look at. Nothing else in the function changes; the query, the args, the scan loop and both output formats are untouched, so no caller can observe a difference other than in the log.

edits.symbol: row-cap unit tests + the call-site test
edits.rationale: Fixtures are the REAL live queries copied verbatim from agent_definitions, not invented shapes — a test built from SQL I wrote to make my own regex pass proves only that. Asserts: the live tool-suggester LIMIT 30 is found; the fetch-one idiom is NOT reported (the signal-to-noise arm, most likely to be simplified away); only a trailing LIMIT counts (subquery, CTE, parameterised, none); trailing semicolon/newline/case still match; equality-or-beyond fires and under-full does not. THE CALL-SITE TEST IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS: sqlmock drives QueryDatabaseAction for real and a zap observer asserts exactly one warning naming the step, plus a negative control that an under-full result stays silent. Without it every other test passes while the action never calls the helper — which is exactly what mutation M7 demonstrated.

The 275 fix itself: `left(description, 200) AS description` and drop `LIMIT 30`. Bounds the payload at the column that IS the payload (description is 80% of it) instead of at coverage. Migration 406's requires-backend gate is preserved byte-for-byte — the bug warns explicitly that 406's gated query is now the base text and not to restore an older ungated sketch, so the only differences from the live string are the left() and the removed LIMIT. Scoped by id with a PRE-STATE GATE that refuses unless the row still carries both the gate and the LIMIT 30, so it cannot clobber a concurrent change by another session — that is the hardened shape 406's own council round asked future agent_definitions migrations to adopt. Verify block is DO/RAISE, never bare SELECTs, because ON_ERROR_STOP ignores a non-empty result and a SELECT-only verify cannot stop the COMMIT.

DB config is LIVE ON APPLY — there is no image roll to gate it and no redeploy that undoes it, so the rollback has to exist before the apply, not after something looks wrong. It carries the SAME pre-state gate shape as the forward migration, refusing unless the row currently carries 445's text, so re-running it cannot silently revert a LATER change some other session made — which is the failure mode a naive rollback has on a tree this many sessions share.
